pages.x: By 1560 perhaps one French person in ten had become a Protestant, a Huguenot, following the teaching of John Calvin, among them many nobles. The king was a boy, and his mother tried to keep the peace between the two faiths. In 1562 the Duke of Guise's men massacred Protestants at worship in a barn at Wassy, and war broke out.

The queen mother, Catherine de' Medici, tried everything: edicts of toleration, peace treaties, and a royal wedding. In August 1572 her daughter Margaret married the young Protestant Henry of Navarre in Paris, and the Huguenot nobility crowded into the city for the celebrations.

Days after the wedding someone shot and wounded the Huguenot leader, Admiral Coligny. Fearing revenge, the king and his mother agreed to strike first. Before dawn on 24 August Coligny was murdered, and Paris mobs hunted down Protestants through the streets. The killing spread to other cities.

The wars went on, with Spain backing the Catholic League and England the Protestants. In 1588 King Henry III had his rival, Henry, Duke of Guise, stabbed to death in his castle at Blois; the next year a monk stabbed the king himself. The heir to the throne was the Protestant Henry of Navarre.

Catholic Paris would not accept a Protestant king, and Henry IV fought for years to win it. In 1593 he became a Catholic. Paris is worth a Mass, he is supposed to have said, though he probably never did. The city opened its gates to him in 1594.

In 1598 Henry signed the Edict of Nantes, which let Protestants worship freely in many places, hold office, and keep their own fortified towns. It was one of the first laws in Europe to let two faiths live side by side in one kingdom. In 1610 Henry was stabbed to death by a Catholic fanatic.

The wars killed perhaps two to four million people, through fighting, hunger and disease. Henry's peace lasted until 1685, when his grandson Louis XIV took back the edict, and some 200,000 Huguenots fled abroad, taking their skills to England, the Netherlands, Prussia and South Africa.
